title: The exam and the bands
summary: After this unit you know exactly how IELTS Academic is structured, how your four papers become one band, and what examiners look for at band 9.

lessons.title: The Academic test, paper by paper

items.title: Four papers, one result
body: IELTS Academic tests Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. The first three are taken in one sitting with no break; Speaking is a separate face-to-face interview with an examiner, held on the same day or within about a week either side.

Each paper gets its own band from 1 to 9 in half-band steps, and the four are combined into one **overall band**. Universities and professional bodies often set a minimum for the overall band *and* for each paper, so a weak paper can sink an otherwise excellent result.
list: Speaking: 11-14 minutes, 3 parts, with an examiner
items.tip: At band 9 there is almost no margin: 39 or 40 correct out of 40 in Listening and Reading. Your preparation is about eliminating slips, not learning new skills.

items.title: Listening
body: You hear each recording **once only**. Part 1 is an everyday conversation between two people (booking, enquiring), Part 2 an everyday monologue (a tour, a talk to visitors), Part 3 an academic discussion with two main speakers, for example students with a tutor, and Part 4 a single-speaker lecture. Difficulty rises from Part 1 to Part 4. Speakers have a range of accents, including British, Australian, New Zealand and North American.

There is time to read the questions before each part, and the questions follow the order of the recording. On computer you type your answers as you listen and have **2 minutes** at the end to review them. (The old paper test gave ten minutes to transfer answers to a separate sheet; that step no longer exists.)

Spelling counts. A correctly heard word that is misspelt scores nothing, and so does an answer that goes over the word limit. A hyphenated word such as *check-in* counts as one word; contracted forms such as *they're* are not tested.

items.title: Reading
body: Three long passages, taken from books, journals, magazines and newspapers and written for a non-specialist audience. They may include diagrams, graphs or illustrations, and any technical term comes with a simple definition. The passages get harder and more argumentative as you go: Passage 3 is often a dense discussion of ideas with the writer's own views woven in.
There is **no extra transfer time**. The 60 minutes include everything, so a realistic plan is about 17, 20 and 23 minutes for the three passages.
The official list has eleven question types, and any of them can appear with any passage:
list: identifying the writer's views or claims (YES / NO / NOT GIVEN)
summary, note, table or flow-chart completion

items.title: Writing
body: **Task 1** (at least 150 words, about 20 minutes): describe and compare the key features of a graph, table, chart, process diagram or map. You report what the data shows; you do not explain causes or give opinions.

**Task 2** (at least 250 words, about 40 minutes): an essay responding to a point of view, argument or problem. Task 2 carries **twice the weight** of Task 1 in the Writing band, so never let Task 1 eat into its time.

Write in full sentences: notes and bullet points are penalised, and so is anything that does not relate to the topic. A response below the minimum may not give enough evidence for the higher bands. Under the band descriptors revised in May 2023, a response of 20 words or fewer is rated band 1, words copied from the question are discounted, and a totally memorised answer gets band 0.
There is no maximum. In our experience 270-320 well-developed words are enough for Task 2; length itself earns nothing.
items.tip: In some locations the British Council offers **Writing on Paper**: you handwrite both tasks while the rest of the test is on computer. The tasks and the marking are the same either way.

items.title: Speaking
body: A recorded conversation of 11-14 minutes with one examiner. **Part 1** (4-5 minutes): short questions on familiar topics such as your work, home or interests. **Part 2** (3-4 minutes in total): a task card, one minute to prepare, then a talk of up to two minutes. **Part 3** (4-5 minutes): a more abstract discussion linked to the Part 2 topic.
The examiner follows a script, so do not read anything into an interruption: it usually means time is up, not that you have done badly.

items.title: Computer delivery and One Skill Retake
body: Paper-based IELTS has ended: IDP announced that from 27 June 2026 all IELTS tests are delivered on computer. The British Council keeps a **Writing on Paper** option in some locations, where you handwrite the Writing tasks and take the rest of the test on computer. Check what your centre offers before booking.
On computer you can highlight text in Reading, see a word count in Writing and move freely between questions within a paper. Results normally arrive within 1-2 days.

**One Skill Retake** lets you resit one paper, rather than all four, within 60 days of your test, once per test. It is not available for IELTS Online. You receive a new Test Report Form and can use either that or the original. UKVI accepts it in selected locations, and each organisation decides whether to accept it, so check with the one that will receive your scores.

items.q: How many times do you hear each Listening recording?
items.why: Every recording is played **once only**, which is why prediction and question-reading time matter so much.

items.statement: Task 1 and Task 2 contribute equally to the Writing band.
items.why: Task 2 carries **twice the weight** of Task 1, so it deserves about 40 of your 60 minutes.

items.q: Which part of the Speaking test gives you one minute to prepare?
items.why: Part 2 is the long turn: you get a task card, one minute to make notes, then speak for up to two minutes.

items.statement: The Reading paper includes ten extra minutes to transfer answers.
items.why: The 60 minutes include everything; there is **no extra transfer time** in Reading.

items.q: What is the minimum length for Task 2?
items.why: Task 2 needs at least 250 words; Task 1 at least 150.

items.statement: One Skill Retake must be taken within 60 days of the original full test.
items.why: One Skill Retake must be taken **within 60 days** of the original test, and only once per test.

items.title: From raw score to band
body: In Listening and Reading every question is worth one mark, and your raw score out of 40 is converted to a band with a conversion table. The conversion is approximate: cut-offs vary slightly between versions of the test. As a guide, for Academic Reading 39-40 correct is band 9, 37-38 is 8.5 and 35-36 is 8, and Listening is almost identical at the top.
So the difference between 8 and 9 is four or five questions across the whole paper. Each careless spelling, plural *s* or extra word costs real money.

items.title: Writing and Speaking bands
body: Writing and Speaking are marked by trained examiners against four criteria, each weighted equally and each given a band. The criterion bands are averaged to give the paper's band.
In Writing, the two tasks are marked separately and combined with Task 2 counting double. A brilliant Task 1 cannot rescue a weak Task 2.

items.title: The overall band and rounding
body: The overall band is the **mean of the four papers**, rounded to the nearest half band. Two rules decide the awkward cases: an average ending in **.25 rounds up to .5**, and an average ending in **.75 rounds up to the next whole band**.
Other averages go to whichever half band is nearer: 8.125 becomes 8, 8.375 becomes 8.5, 8.625 becomes 8.5 and 8.875 becomes 9.

examples.text: Listening 9, Reading 9, Writing 8, Speaking 8.5: mean 8.625, overall 8.5
Listening 9, Reading 8.5, Writing 8, Speaking 7.5: mean 8.25, overall 8.5
Listening 9, Reading 9, Writing 8.5, Speaking 8.5: mean 8.75, overall 9
examples.note: .75 rounds up to the next whole band.

items.title: Bands and the CEFR
body: IELTS maps its bands onto the Common European Framework of Reference. According to ielts.org, **8.5-9 is C2**, with 8 on the borderline of C2, and the C1 threshold lies between 6.5 and 7: many candidates with 6.5 are at C1, but some fall just below it. Lower down the scale, the mapping is looser. Your target is therefore not 'more C1' but a different kind of control.
The mapping is approximate and institutions publish their own requirements, so treat it as orientation, not a guarantee.

items.title: What a 7, an 8 and a 9 look like
body: **Band 7, good user:** copes well with complex language and detailed reasoning, but slips and the odd misunderstanding still appear, especially on unfamiliar ground.
**Band 8, very good user:** in control almost everywhere; errors are occasional and random rather than patterned, and only an unusual situation causes a misunderstanding.
**Band 9, expert user:** complete command. Language is accurate, appropriate and fluent, comprehension is total, and any error is so rare that it reads as a slip, never as a gap in knowledge.

The 8-to-9 step is about **consistency**: a band 8 writer produces band 9 sentences most of the time, but an odd awkward collocation, a slightly mechanical linker or an underdeveloped point keeps the script at 8.

items.q: A candidate gets 36 out of 40 in Academic Reading. Which band is that?
items.why: 35-36 correct converts to **band 8**; two more marks would have meant 8.5.

items.q: Listening 8.5, Reading 9, Writing 7.5, Speaking 8. What is the overall band?
items.why: The sum is 33, so the mean is 8.25, and an average ending in **.25 rounds up** to 8.5. Note that 8.25 is never reported: bands go in half steps.

items.q: Listening 9, Reading 9, Writing 8, Speaking 8. What is the overall band?
items.why: The mean is 8.5 exactly, so the overall band is 8.5.

items.q: Listening 9, Reading 9, Writing 8.5, Speaking 8.5. What is the overall band?
items.why: The mean is 8.75, and an average ending in **.75 rounds up** to the next whole band: 9.

items.statement: In the Writing paper, Task 1 and Task 2 bands are simply averaged.
items.why: Task 2 counts **double**, so the combination is weighted, not a simple average.

items.q: Which CEFR level does IELTS band 8.5-9 broadly correspond to?
items.why: 8.5-9 is **C2** (8 is borderline C2), and the C1 threshold lies between 6.5 and 7. The mapping is approximate.

items.title: Writing: four criteria, equal weight
body: Every Writing task is marked on four criteria worth 25% each. Knowing what each one rewards tells you where your marks are leaking.

items.title: Task Achievement and Task Response
body: Task 1: do you select the **key features**, give a clear overview and support it with accurate data? Band 9 covers everything the task requires with a fully developed, precisely judged response; nothing important is missing and nothing trivial clutters it.

Task 2: do you answer **every part of the question**, take a clear position that holds throughout and develop ideas with relevant, extended support? At band 9 the answer is fully on target: an unaddressed sub-question or a drifting conclusion is enough to cap the criterion lower.

items.title: Coherence and Cohesion
body: How easily the reader follows you: logical sequencing, paragraphing that groups one central idea each, and cohesive devices (reference, substitution, linkers) that do their job without being noticed.

Band 9 is cohesion that **attracts no attention**. Overused 'Furthermore… Moreover… In addition' is a band 6-7 habit; a band 9 writer leans on reference ('this shift', 'such schemes') and on the logic of the ideas themselves.

items.title: Lexical Resource
body: Range, precision and naturalness of vocabulary: collocation, register, idiomatic usage, spelling and word formation.

Band 9 means a wide range used with **full flexibility and precise meaning**, with only the rarest slips. Rare words are not the goal. 'The policy backfired' beats 'the policy engendered deleterious ramifications', which is the kind of forced choice examiners notice.

items.title: Grammatical Range and Accuracy
body: The variety of structures you control (subordination, conditionals, passives, relative and participle clauses, nominalisation) and how accurate they are, punctuation included.
Band 9 uses a wide range with full flexibility; **errors are rare** and read as slips. A band 8 script typically has a handful of minor errors in otherwise complex writing; band 9 has almost none.

items.title: Speaking: four criteria, equal weight
body: **Fluency and Coherence**: speaking at length without effort, hesitating only to think about content rather than to search for words, and linking ideas clearly.
**Lexical Resource**: flexible, precise, idiomatic vocabulary on every topic, including the ability to paraphrase when a word escapes you.
**Grammatical Range and Accuracy**: a full range of structures used naturally and accurately, apart from the kind of slips native speakers also make.

**Pronunciation**: the full range of features (stress, rhythm, intonation, connected speech) used precisely and flexibly, so that you are effortless to understand. An accent is **not** penalised; unclear or monotonous delivery is.

items.title: What band 9 does not mean
body: It does not mean sounding British, using idioms in every answer or never pausing. Natural speakers pause to think. The difference is that a band 9 speaker pauses for ideas, never for words, and the idioms they use are apt and unforced.
It does not mean long, ornate sentences in Writing either. Range is shown by choosing the right structure for each idea, which sometimes means a short one.

items.q: A Task 2 essay ignores the second half of a two-part question. Which criterion is hit hardest?
items.why: Not addressing all parts of the task is a **Task Response** problem, and it caps that criterion however good the language is.

items.statement: A strong regional or foreign accent lowers the Pronunciation band by itself.
items.why: Accent is not penalised; what matters is how **easy to understand** you are and how well you use stress, rhythm and intonation.

items.q: Which habit is most typical of a band 6-7 writer rather than a band 9 writer?
options: Using reference words such as 'this trend'
Using a single central idea per paragraph
items.why: Mechanical, overused linkers are a classic mid-band feature; band 9 cohesion **attracts no attention**.

items.q: In Speaking Fluency and Coherence, which kind of hesitation is consistent with band 9?
options: Pausing to search for a word
Pausing to decide what to say next
items.why: At the top band hesitation is **content-related**, not caused by searching for language.

items.statement: Each of the four Writing criteria carries equal weight.
items.why: The four criteria are weighted **equally**, 25% each, for both tasks.

items.q: Which choice best reflects band 9 Lexical Resource?
options: 'The scheme had very very bad results.'
'The scheme was a bad thing that happened.'
items.why: Band 9 rewards **precise, natural** vocabulary; the first option is forced and overblown, the others are imprecise.
